meta.title: Cantonese B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 939 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Cantonese → English (see the Cantonese, recall the meaning) and English → Cantonese (see an English meaning, recall the Cantonese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 939 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in their field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. THIS IS SPOKEN HONG KONG CANTONESE, the language people talk in, not the written Chinese Hong Kong reads and writes, which is close to Mandarin: 佢 for he or she, 喺 for at, 嘢 for a thing, 睇 to look, and the sentence-final particles that carry a Cantonese speaker's tone of voice. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no examination publishes a graded word list for Cantonese, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 804 of the 939 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — politics and public administration (the Legislative Council, the Basic Law), the law and the courts, the economy, business and finance, science and research, technology and the internet, the environment and natural resources, health, medicine and the mind, the arts, literature, Cantonese opera and the media, history and society (public housing, the MPF, subdivided flats), argument and evaluation, the formal connectors, the verbs of reporting, analysing and persuading, and the colloquial expressions of everyday Hong Kong speech — and the other 135 are the commonest remaining words of spoken Cantonese, counted in the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus (recorded conversations and radio, 1997–98). The cards are dealt by how often the words are heard there and in Tatoeba's Cantonese sentences, so the commonest come first. THIS LEVEL IS SHORT of the 1,500 words planned for it: the spoken corpus has no more words that the levels below have not taught, and the rest of the level is the vocabulary written for its topics, so the deck stops where the sources do rather than take words from written Chinese or from a machine's word count. Every headword is printed in the traditional characters Hong Kong uses, with the simplified form beneath where it differs, and in Jyutping, the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong's romanisation, which ends every syllable with its TONE as a digit: 1 high, 2 high rising, 3 mid, 4 low falling, 5 low rising, 6 low — because a Cantonese syllable said on the wrong tone is a different word (si1 poem, si4 time, si6 yes). The Cantonese Jyutping and Tones deck, the first in this collection, teaches the sounds and the six tones. The part of speech is the one the corpus's annotators gave the word, and the classifiers a noun is counted with are taught as words of their own rather than printed on the noun. Example sentences come with 96 of the 939 words, three apiece for 7 of them — Tatoeba's Cantonese is small, so many words have none — with the word picked out in colour, a speaker beside each sentence, and the Jyutping beneath it where every word in the sentence carries a reading the dictionaries confirm. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings: CC-CEDICT (MDBG, CC BY-SA 4.0) and CC-Canto (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0). Jyutping: CC-Canto and its Cantonese readings of CC-CEDICT (Pleco, CC BY-SA 3.0), and the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus. Frequency and parts of speech: the Hong Kong Cantonese Corpus, HKCanCor (Luke Kang Kwong; CC BY 4.0, as distributed with PyCantonese), and Tatoeba. Example sentences and their Jyutping: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
